title: Family & Friends 2

subtitle.text: Ethan was driving with Dad in the mountains.
Dad was excited about their spring camping trip.
He loved the outdoors, and this was his favorite time of year.
Ethan didn't really like camping though.
He preferred to stay indoors and solve brainteasers.
"Isn't nature beautiful?" asked Dad.
"Yep," muttered Ethan.
"Camping is a lot of work," Dad went on.
"But spending time outdoors is fun.
Remember, don't disturb nature during our trip, okay?"
"No problem!" said Ethan.
He tried to ignore nature as much as possible—especially all the bugs in the woods.
He stared out the window at the boring scenery.
Just then he spotted something strange.
Up ahead, next to the roadside barrier, a deer was frantically pacing back and forth.
"I think something's wrong," said Ethan. "Dad, pull over!"
"That's not a good idea," said Dad.
"It's best to leave wild animals alone."
"Please, Dad. Pull over!" Ethan repeated.
"The deer looks upset."
Reluctantly, Dad parked on the side of the road and turned on the car's hazard lights.
The two of them got out and slowly approached the deer.
It appeared afraid, but it didn't run away.
"Look!" yelled Ethan, pointing to a ditch below.
A young fawn was standing in a rushing stream.
"The deer's fawn is stuck down there. We have to save it!"
Dad shook his head.
"There's nothing we can do.
This slope is too steep for us."
Ethan spotted the forest ranger's number on a nearby sign.
He called the number and explained the situation.
Soon Tucker, the forest ranger, arrived.
He looked down into the ditch and frowned.
"I can't get down there by myself," he said.
Ethan nervously watched the stream's current.
It was moving faster and nearly knocked the fawn over.
"Maybe we can think of another solution," Ethan blurted out.
"What if we formed a human chain? We could pull the fawn up."
"That might work," said Tucker.
"But we're going to need more adults."
"I'll get help from passing cars!" said Dad.
After Dad got five people to help, Tucker decided to begin the rescue.
"I'll take the lead," said Tucker.
Everyone joined hands.
Ethan stood with his Dad at the end of the chain.
Dad gripped the man ahead of him with one hand while his other hand gripped the roadside barrier.
The human chain carefully descended.
At the bottom of the ditch, Tucker broke off from the group and went toward the fawn.
He gently scooped it up and carried it back to the chain.
One man grabbed onto Tucker's waist, and they all began to pull upward.
Ethan let out a sigh of relief.
Finally the people—and the fawn—were back at the top.
The fawn squirmed out of Tucker's arms and dashed toward its mother.
Then the deer disappeared into the woods.
"Nice job, Ethan," said Dad.
"I told you to leave nature alone.
But I guess nature needs help from humans sometimes."
The ranger nodded.
"The human chain was a smart idea.
You're obviously a nature lover."
"Um . . ." Ethan grinned, and Dad burst out laughing.
"I guess I am!"
Last week was my birthday.
My parents gave me a cool gift—my own smartphone.
"Enjoying your new phone, Ella?" Dad asked.
"Don't forget your online manners.
"Number one: Think before you send or post."
I groaned as Dad started listing our family's "netiquette rules."
"Two: Never chat or share pictures with strangers . . ."
By now I'd heard these rules a million times.
While Dad continued reciting them, I looked down at my phone.
I had a new message from my friend, Josh.
Josh: Hey! Still want to go to the movies tomorrow?
Ella: Yes!
Josh: Great! Violet?
I rolled my eyes.
Josh, Violet, and I had been friends since third grade.
But things started to change when we entered middle school.
Violet had joined the drama club and made new friends. Now
whenever she hung around with us, she sang songs from musicals—loudly. It
got on my nerves. "Ella?"
"Oops,
sorry, Dad. Josh asked me something." He
frowned. "Dad,
you don't have to tell me about netiquette again," I said quickly. "Trust
me—I know all the rules already." "Good."
He nodded. "Then
it's time to follow rule number five: no screen time until your chores are done." I
saluted him. "Got it." Ella:
No Violet tomorrow. I'm sick of her loud singing! I
inserted an emoticon with a person plugging her ears, and then I went to fold laundry. ***
The next day when I met Josh at the movie theater, he rushed up to me.
"So, is Violet really angry?"
"Angry about what?" I asked.
"About what you said about her."
"I don't know what you're talking about."
Josh looked worried.
"Yesterday when we were talking, it was a group chat."
I blinked. "Does that mean . . .?"
"Yep, Violet was in our chat too."
Josh and I bought tickets and sat down.
He started laughing at something on his phone, but I was too anxious to laugh at anything.
I was thinking about how I'd insulted Violet.
No Violet tomorrow. I'm sick of her loud singing!
I felt terrible. Violet and I had grown apart, but she was still my friend.
"Rule number one," I thought as tears slipped down my cheeks.
"Think before you send."
*** After the movie I biked over to Violet’s
house. "I'm sorry, Violet," I blurted
out. "I didn't realize it was a group chat and . . ." I kept talking, desperately trying to apologize.
Violet looked away. "It's okay."
I shook my head. "No, it's not."
We stood in silence for a few moments, and then Violet looked up.
"You definitely hurt my feelings, Ella.
But my family says I do talk about theater stuff too much."
She flashed a weak smile at me.
"I'll try to stop singing show tunes, I promise."
"I made such a stupid mistake," I mumbled.
Violet nodded. "My parents always say to be cautious online.
You can't take something back once you send it or post it."
I swallowed. I'd learned that lesson the hard way.
She shrugged and opened the door wider.
"Want to come in for a while?"
"Sure." I turned off my phone and then went inside.
Pizza boxes and soda cans cover the table.
The video game team has been working hard!
Julie, the game designer, leads the team.
The game designer is responsible for how the game works.
Some games are simple—pop the balloons!
Other games tell stories with characters, like stick figures looking for a snack.
Stories can get complex too, with huge worlds and lots of characters.
The designer decides what can happen in the game world.
Julie's team is making Treasure Hunter , an adventure
game. The hero is searching around the world for ancient
treasure. She uses a storyboard—a series of pictures—to introduce her ideas to the
team. Today the team is planning a new
level. The hero will go through a
swamp! The hero needs new tools: scuba gear and insect
spray. After the meeting everyone has a job to
do. What will the swamp and the characters look
like? This job is for the
artists. They also need to draw the new tools and
backgrounds. The artists use computers to draw everything in the
game. The programmers write the computer code that runs the
game. The code counts the game points.
It also controls what the game player sees.
The programmers make sure the game works correctly.
When the hero jumps, he has to follow the correct path.
Then he has to land in the right spot.
The game needs sound too.
The audio crew is responsible for any sounds the game makes.
The swamp level needs new sounds.
Splash! That's the sound for landing in the muddy water.
Hsst! That's the sound for using bug spray.
Sometimes the audio crew can use real sounds for the game sounds.
The insect spray sound is easy.
But making other sounds is more difficult.
Why is the crew blowing bubbles with straws?
They're making the sound for the scuba gear!
Whew! The testers have spent hours playing the new level.
They tell Julie what they liked and didn't like.
They say the swamp level is a great level!
But there are a few bugs to fix.
Sometimes the insect spray doesn't work!
The testers tell the programmers about the bugs.
Their work is done for now.
Julie's work isn't done, though.
She already has ideas for the next level!
The Pop-Song Crew's leadership committee was finishing up their monthly meeting.
The Pop-Song Crew was the school singing club.
"Is there anything else to discuss?" Jerry, the club's president, asked.
"No," Lucy, the treasurer, replied.
Kathy, the secretary, shook her head.
"Yes!" Mrs. Mayer, the club's faculty advisor, said eagerly.
She was looking at her phone.
"We've been invited to sing at the Newtown Spring Festival next month."
The kids cheered.
"I can't wait to tell the rest of the club members," Jerry said.
"Wait," Lucy said.
"Newtown is three hours away.
We'd have to rent a van to get there."
"How much did it cost last time we rented a van?" Mrs. Mayer asked.
Lucy checked the club's account.
"Three hundred dollars. Plus $35 for gas.
We only have twenty dollars left in our account."
She did a quick calculation.
"We'd have to raise $315."
Kathy groaned.
"We can ask everyone in the club to pitch in," Jerry suggested. Lucy
punched the numbers into the calculator app on her phone. "With
11 members, everyone would have to pay $28.63 each." "That's
a lot for some members," Mrs. Mayer said. "Especially
since we've had many expenses this year." "We
could hold a fundraiser," Kathy suggested. "Great
idea," Jerry said. "How about a car wash?" "Math
Club had one last week," Lucy said. "A
bake sale?" Kathy asked. "We'd
have to sell a lot of cookies to raise $315." Lucy sighed. "Can
we text about this later?" Kathy asked. "I'm
late for a friend's birthday party at the bowling alley." "Hey!
Science Club did a bowling fundraiser last year," Jerry said. "They
raised a lot of money." "I'll
call and find out the costs," Lucy said. "Then
we can figure out a budget." ***
The next day Lucy sent a group text to the committee.
"Bad news. The bowling alley costs two hundred dollars to rent for two hours.
That means we'd have to raise $515 total."
"Now what?" Jerry texted back.
Lucy sent a shrugging emoticon.
Ten minutes later Kathy texted.
"Can you meet me at the bowling alley?
I think I have a solution!"
*** When Lucy and Jerry arrived at the bowling alley, Kathy introduced them to her friend
Carl. "I'm a big fan of your club!" Carl
said. "My uncle owns this bowling
alley. He said he'd only charge you one hundred dollars for three
hours. And the rental fee includes the games and shoe
rentals. He thinks this would be great publicity for the bowling
alley." "That means we'd need to raise $415 total," Lucy
said. "If we charge $10 per person, we'll need at least 42 people to come to our fundraiser."
"What if all eleven club members bring three people with them?" Jerry suggested.
"That's 44 people," Kathy said.
"We'd raise $440!" Lucy said. "That’s more than enough!"
"This is great, Carl," Jerry said. "Thank you!"
*** Two weeks later Lucy, Jerry, and Mrs. Mayer sat at a table in the bowling alley.
The fundraiser had been a lot of fun.
Even more people had shown up than they had expected.
"How much did we make?" Kathy asked.
Lucy finished counting the money.
"We made $560.
After we pay $100 to the bowling alley, we have a profit of $460.
That covers the costs of the van and gas, and we'll have $125 left over."
"Plus, the twenty dollars in our account," Mrs. Mayer said.
"We can buy lunch for everyone on the trip."
Jerry smiled. "Thanks to Carl and his uncle, The Pop-Song Crew is going to Newtown!"
"Finally!" Maddie said as Gage skidded into the yard.
"You're twenty minutes late!"
"Football practice ran late again, sorry!"
Gage started madly raking leaves.
Maddie sighed.
Gage was small and shy, and he had never been into sports before.
But this year he seemed to care about nothing else.
"How was practice?" she asked, trying to sound supportive.
He grinned. "Great. I'm the fastest runner on the team."
"Cool." Maddie just wished he was a little faster at getting to their after-school job.
They were helping their neighbor, Mrs. Famer, with some yard work for an hour a few days every week.
"Ready to trim those tree branches?"
"Sure." Gage grabbed the shears and raced up the ladder.
As Maddie picked up the branches he cut, frustrated thoughts crowded her mind.
If Gage had been on time, they might have been finished by now.
The ladder suddenly shook, and a branch flew past her head.
"What are you doing up there?"
"Just practicing a football pass." Gage sounded embarrassed.
"I guess it works better on the ground."
Maddie bit back angry words.
At this rate trimming the trees was going to take twice as long as it should.
Sure enough, their hour of work was up before the trees were done.
But Mrs. Famer thanked and paid them.
She smiled at Gage.
"You must have a different schedule these days.
You two never show up at the same time anymore."
"I know," Gage mumbled guiltily.
As she and Gage walked home, Maddie clutched the money in her hand.
Normally, she halved it right away.
"You've been late a lot, Gage!" she finally blurted out.
"Football just . . ." Gage's voice trailed away.
All of Maddie's frustration bubbled up.
"Football!" she exploded.
"Is that the most important thing in the world now?
You don't care about your friends, or doing a good job?
I wish you'd never made the team!"
Gage winced. "I'm really sorry," he said.
Maddie deflated.
Gage looked hurt now, and she wished she hadn't lost her temper.
She took a deep breath, fighting to keep her voice calm.
"I've been working the full hour we promised Mrs. Famer.
You've been coming late, but still getting half the money. It isn't fair."
"You're right," Gage said.
"You should keep all the money, Maddie.
I just don't think I can get here any earlier."
"I don't want all the money," she murmured.
"You earned some of it."
She carefully divided the handful of dollar bills—two thirds for herself, one third for Gage.
"Do you think that's fair?" she asked awkwardly.
He nodded, looking more embarrassed than ever.
Maddie tried to fill the uncomfortable silence.
"It's not much fun, working by myself," she said.
"I wish we could—hey!" She had a sudden thought.
"Maybe we could work more on the weekend and less during the week.
Then you wouldn't be late, and we could split everything half and half again!"
Gage hesitated.
"Sometimes I have football games on Saturdays. Could we work around that?"
Maddie held out her hand. "Let's try. Deal?"
They shook on it.
"Now I won't have to feel bad about being late anymore," Gage added.
"I didn't want to cancel on you completely."
"You always seem so happy after practice," Maddie said.
"I didn't want to ruin it with a big argument—"
"Until you started yelling about football today?" Gage gave her a small smile.
"Next time, tell me what the problem is before you get all mad."
Maddie grinned. "That's a deal too!"
Morgan was walking her dog, Pip, with her friend Rasha.
Suddenly a big dog raced toward them, barking loudly.
Pip pulled hard on his leash.
Then, before Morgan could tighten her grip, the leash flew from her hand.
As Pip took off toward the playground, the big dog ran after him, growling and barking.
The two dogs tore around the slide, through the sandbox, and around the swings.
Then Pip darted toward the tennis court.
"I've got him!" a tennis player called, grabbing Pip's leash.
"Whew!" Morgan ran over and scooped up her dog. "Thank you!"
A young guy with a skateboard appeared and whistled at the big dog. "Dakota! Come!"
"Hey!" Morgan called.
"Your dog chased my dog all over the park!"
"Relax, kid. It's totally fine."
"No, it's not!" Rasha said.
"Pip could have gotten bitten, or he could have run out into the street!
You should keep your dog on a leash!"
Dakota ran off again, chasing a squirrel this time.
The skateboarder shrugged.
Then he dropped his board and skated away.
Morgan could still feel her heart thumping in her chest.
"That was terrifying."
"We need to do something!" Rasha fumed.
"Our city doesn't have a leash law.
Let's tell the city council to enact one.
It's not safe for dogs to run loose in the park."
"Um, there's just one problem," Morgan said.
"We're kids. Who's going to listen to us?"
"In a democracy we have rights too," Rasha said.
"Besides, my mom used to work at City Hall.
So I have some ideas!"
Morgan and Rasha got busy.
First, they sent a letter to the newspaper about why their city needed a leash law to keep dogs safe.
Next, they sent emails to friends and neighbors, asking them to call local politicians.
After that, they created a petition.
"We need to collect lots of signatures," Rasha said.
"That will show the city council that lots of citizens want a leash law."
Morgan and Rasha brought the petition to locations all over the city.
Some people said they didn't want to sign it.
"My dog likes to run without a leash."
"We already have too many rules!"
But others were eager to sign.
One man even nodded after Morgan told him about how Dakota had chased Pip.
"I've seen Dakota running wild through the park," he said.
"Where do I sign?"
The following week Rasha's mom drove the girls to City Hall for a city council meeting.
The girls waited for their turn to speak.
"You have five minutes," the president said.
Rasha explained why the city needed a leash law to protect dogs and dog owners.
Then Morgan held up their petition.
"We collected hundreds of signatures.
Lots of people want a leash law."
The president nodded.
"We've gotten dozens of calls."
Another council member frowned.
"I have more important things to do," he muttered.
"Protecting kids' dogs is a waste of my time."
"Thank you for bringing this issue to our attention, girls," the president said.
"We'll vote on it at our next meeting."
Morgan sighed as she sat down. "What now?"
"We wait," Rasha said. "Change never happens overnight."
A month later the girls were walking Pip in the park.
"Look!" Rasha pointed to a workman posting a sign.
"All dogs must be on a leash.
Violators will be fined."
She hugged Morgan.
"We did it!" Morgan cheered.
Zoe was listening to Chase Gibson's newest song while doing research for her hero project.
Her project partner, Amanda, had already made a list of possible heroes—all politicians, artists, and scientists.
"Boring," Zoe thought after reading about Amanda's fifth-choice pick.
Amanda had already said no to Zoe's first choice—Chase Gibson.
He was her favorite singer.
And he could dance and act too.
"But how has he changed the world?" Amanda had asked at school that day. "Besides,
I read he isn't even that nice." Zoe
didn't care. Maybe
she could still persuade Amanda that Chase was talented enough to write about. Taking
a break, she pulled up the official Chase Gibson fan website. She
could hardly believe her eyes. "Aaah!"
Zoe's scream echoed through the house. "Zoe,
what's wrong? What happened?" Zoe
turned around to see Mom in the doorway. "Chase
Gibson is coming to the mall this Saturday to sign autographs!" Mom
frowned. "Never scream like that, unless you're hurt or in danger." "Can
I go? Please, Mom!" "You
and Amanda are working on your project on Saturday," Mom said. "Schoolwork
comes first, you know." "But
Mom!" Zoe pleaded. "Zoe,
no," Mom said firmly. "Now
turn that music down please. Dinner will be ready soon." Zoe
slouched down and lowered the volume as Mom headed downstairs. "I have
to go to the mall this Saturday," she thought. *** After
waiting in line for over an hour, Zoe finally stepped up to the table. Seeing
Chase Gibson in person made her forget all about the big lie she'd told her mother. "Hi,
Chase! I'm your biggest fan!" Zoe said to the star. "Can
you sign some things To Zoe , without a y
?" She emptied her backpack filled with Chase Gibson merchandise onto the
table. Chase Gibson looked at Zoe and then at the pile of
stuff. "I can't sign all that!" he
snapped. "I've been signing autographs for
hours! And look at that
line!" Zoe felt a lump in her throat. "But I'm
your—" "Biggest fan? Yes, I know. That's what everyone
says. Now pick one thing, and I'll sign it.
Let's keep this line moving."
Zoe shyly unrolled a small poster.
Chase Gibson quickly scribbled an autograph on it.
As Zoe walked away from the table, she looked at the autograph:
To Zoey, —Chase Gibson it read in big ugly letters. "Ugh."
Just then her phone beeped.
It was a text message from Mom.
Come home right now!
*** "You lied about where you were going!" Mom's eyes
narrowed. "I had no idea where you were when Amanda's mom
called! Then I remembered that Chase Gibson was at the mall
today." Zoe winced at hearing that name. "I'm sorry,
Mom." "I'll talk with you about some consequences
later. For now, go to your
room. Amanda will be here soon to work on your
project. I hope you've learned a
lesson!" "Oh, I learned a big lesson today," Zoe murmured.
Zoe trudged off to her room.
She flung her backpack, still filled with Chase Gibson stuff, onto the floor.
She reached for her notebook.
A Chase Gibson sticker smiled at her on the cover.
Zoe stared back at him.
"I still like your music.
But Amanda was right—you're not a hero."
She flipped open the notebook and began searching for a hero from Amanda's list.
Hank frowned at the sketch on his desk.
His class was having a T-shirt contest for Earth Day, and each student had to create a logo.
Then Mrs. Getty would choose a winner and order T-shirts for everyone.
Hank had sketched a green frog with a speech bubble that read Think Green.
But he didn't like his design very much.
He added a superhero cape and a new speech bubble: Fight for Earth.
"That's better," he thought. "But—"
Anna suddenly poked him with her pencil.
"Cool logo," she whispered.
"Thanks." Hank was still frowning. "I don't like it."
"I do. I hate to draw and—"
"Anna and Hank!" Mrs. Getty said sharply.
"You're supposed to be writing book reviews—not talking."
"Sorry," Hank mumbled.
"It's time for math now," the teacher said to the class. "You
can finish your reviews later—for homework." Everyone
groaned. As
Hank flipped his notebook closed, a burst of air sent papers flying off his desk. Sighing,
he scooped them up. "Ugh,"
he thought. He
hadn't even finished reading his book yet. Writing
this dumb book review would take forever. ***
Hank started his homework right after dinner, but as he read, his thoughts kept drifting to the T-shirt contest.
"I'll just draw for a few minutes," he thought.
"Then I'll finish reading."
Hank quickly sketched some ideas.
Next he used colored pencils to add color and details to several designs.
He didn't notice the time until his phone suddenly beeped.
"Ack!" he cried.
"My book review! I lost track of time!"
Hank reached for his phone.
Before he could stop himself, he searched the internet for the title of his book.
A link popped up, which took him to a website . . . with hundreds of book reviews.
"Perfect," he whispered.
He began copying a review into his notebook, and fifteen minutes later his homework was done.
*** On Friday afternoon Mrs. Getty stood at the front of the
room. "It's time to announce our contest
winner." "Yes!" Hank pumped his
fist. "All the designs are wonderful." She flashed a smile at
Hank. "Some are very
elaborate. But I chose one that will work well on a
T-shirt. The winner is . . .
Anna!" "Anna?" Hank gasped as Mrs. Getty held up Anna's
design. "Huh?" Hank
blinked. Anna's logo was a frog in a superhero
cape! At recess Hank stalked over to Anna.
"You stole my design!"
Anna's face turned red.
"I'm sorry, Hank! Your sketch fell on the floor, and you said you didn't like it. So—"
"So you stole it!" Hank snapped.
"Don't you know it's wrong to steal other people's ideas?
It's called plagiarism!"
Anna bit her lip. "I'll tell Mrs. Getty after recess."
"Good!"
When they got back to the classroom, Anna started slowly toward the teacher.
Hank watched her.
"I'm glad Mrs. Getty will find out that I designed that logo," he thought.
Just then his eyes landed on his notebook, and he felt a jolt.
"I stole someone's ideas too," he realized.
"I plagiarized my book review."
Hank stood up, grabbing his notebook.
He needed to talk to Mrs. Getty too.
Noah's grandma was moving into an apartment.
He and his parents were going to her house to help her clean up and pack.
"I hope this doesn't take all day," Noah thought on the drive over.
"I have lots of stuff," Grandma said when they arrived.
"I have some things that you'll be very excited about, Noah."
Noah smiled politely.
Grandma really did have lots of stuff.
But it was mostly dishes, vases, and old pictures.
None of that was exciting.
Mom and Dad started sorting items in the living room.
Grandma was going to take some of those things to her new apartment.
She was going to donate the rest of them.
"Come with me, Noah," Grandma said.
"I have something to show you."
They went into a small room.
Noah saw lots of long, white boxes.
"What's in those boxes?" he asked.
"See for yourself," Grandma said.
Noah opened a box.
It was filled with comic books.
Each was wrapped in plastic.
"I didn't know you liked comic books, Grandma!"
Grandma chuckled.
"I've been collecting them since I was a little girl.
Some are pretty old. Most are in mint condition though."
"What does that mean?" Noah asked.
"Comic books are graded on their condition," Grandma said.
"If a comic book is torn or damaged, it's in poor condition.
When a comic book still looks brand-new, it's in mint condition."
"If a comic book is in mint condition, is it worth a lot of money?" Noah asked. "Sometimes,"
Grandma said. "A
comic book's value depends on different things. Some
comic books are rare. Some
contain the first appearance of a superhero. Others
were illustrated by a famous artist. Those
comic books can be very valuable. Of
course, a comic book is only worth the price someone is willing to pay for it." Grandma
took out a small box and unlocked it. "These
are my most valuable comic books. This
one is the first issue of Super Comics .
And this one is the first issue where the Human Spider had his black costume.
Before that he always wore a purple costume."
"Wow!" Noah said. "I love the Human Spider!"
Grandma smiled. "I'm going to give most of my collection to you."
Noah was shocked. "Really?"
Grandma nodded.
She locked the small box and rested her hand on it. "But not these."
"Oh, okay," Noah murmured.
He felt a little disappointed.
Why couldn't he have those comic books?
Grandma must have known what he was thinking.
"The comic books in this box are worth a fortune, Noah.
I'm going to sell them.
The money will help pay for your college education."
"I might not be able to go to college, Grandma."
Grandma raised an eyebrow. "What do you mean?"
Noah grinned. "I'll be too busy reading the rest of your comic books!"
Grandma laughed. "Very funny, Noah!"
Julie and Doug arrived at Tim's house very excited.
The three friends were going to hear Lisa Byrd sing.
Lisa was a famous performer.
"I can't believe Lisa grew up in our town!" said Julie.
"Her parents own the Byrd Music School where she is performing," said Tim.
"I can't believe our parents are letting us go alone!" said Doug.
"It's not very far," said Tim, rolling his wheelchair to his desk.
"I take piano lessons there every week."
Tim opened a map on his desk.
He followed the streets on the map with his finger.
"You go north on Oak Street, turn east on Elm Drive, then north on Maple Street."
"Here's a shortcut!" said Doug.
He pointed to a path through the park.
"That's not a shorter route," said Tim.
"The streets are straight. The path in the park is squiggly."
"A straight line is the shortest distance between two points," said Julie.
Doug looked at both routes on the map.
"I still think it's shorter to go across the park."
"Hmm," said Julie.
"The shortest distance across an area is a diagonal."
She looked unsure. "Let's measure the length of each route on the map."
Tim picked up a ruler. "I'll measure the streets," he said.
Julie wrote down the lengths of the streets.
Then she added them together.
"The street route is ten centimeters."
"The map scale shows that each centimeter equals two hundred meters," said Tim.
"So it's two kilometers along the streets."
Doug tried to measure the park path.
"It's hard to follow the squiggly line with the ruler."
Tim shook his head. "That won't work."
"I have an idea!" said Julie.
She laid a piece of string over the path.
Then she marked the path's beginning and end on the string.
"Now we can just measure the string!"
Julie stretched the string straight.
Then Doug used the ruler to measure the distance between the two marks.
"It's two kilometers. The same distance as the street route!"
The three kids looked at each other.
"Which way should we go?" asked Tim.
"Through the park!" said Julie. She grinned.
"We can hear the birds sing before we hear Lisa Byrd!"
My dad works as an architect.
A long time ago, he drew a plan for our family's dream house.
Last year he finally began building the house.
The house has three bedrooms and two bathrooms.
It's almost done now.
But I remember every step of building it.
First a bulldozer came and cleared away some trees and rocks.
Then the workers poured concrete for the foundation.
The foundation is what the house sits on.
Next a crew of carpenters cut wood to make the frame.
Then the workers put up the frame.
The frame is like a skeleton for the house.
It holds up the walls and roof.
When the frame was finished, workers added boards to the roof and outside walls.
They also put on the roofing.
Then the plumber and electrician came.
The plumber set up pipes for water.
The electrician put in wires so we could have electricity.
After that the workers added boards to the inside walls.
They also put in the doors and windows.
Every house needs those things, of course!
The workers also put bricks on the outside of the house.
The house looked almost finished from the outside.
But the inside wasn't ready yet.
The workers had to finish the bathrooms and kitchen.
The next part was the most fun for me.
I picked one of the rooms for my bedroom.
Then I got to paint it by myself!
Dad let me choose any color paint I wanted.
I picked blue since it's my favorite color.
In the backyard my parents and I planted bushes and flowers.
The yard already had a tall oak tree.
My brother and I hung a swing from one of its branches.
Whee! Mom and Dad like to swing on it too!
Soon the inspector will come.
He will check everything to make sure the house is safe.
Now our house looks beautiful.
After we move in, we'll have a big party with our new neighbors.
Soon Dad's dream house will be our new home!
Jessica hurried into the barn for her riding lesson and ran straight to her favorite horse's stall.
But Buster's stall was empty.
"Buster's not feeling well," said Mr. Petersen, the riding instructor.
"I'll get Ginger ready for your lesson."
Jessica was worried. "What's wrong with Buster?"
"That's what I'm here to find out," Dr. Roy said as he walked into the barn.
"Come with me."
Jessica followed the vet to where Buster was.
"Mr. Petersen said Buster hasn't been very active for a few days now," Dr. Roy said.
Buster stood still, his head down, as Dr. Roy ran his hands over him.
"Hmm. No sore spots."
Jessica watched the vet examine the horse.
"Mr. Petersen mentioned Buster hasn't had much appetite," he said.
"Horses can easily get upset stomachs.
Their stomachs are small compared to their bodies."
Dr. Roy listened to Buster's stomach with a stethoscope.
"The good news is that Buster's stomach sounds normal."
Next Dr. Roy checked Buster's eyes.
"How did you become a veterinarian?" Jessica asked.
"I studied science for four years in college," said Dr. Roy.
"After I graduated, I went to veterinary school."
"How long did that take?" Jessica asked.
"Four years. Then I had to pass a test to get my veterinarian's license."
Dr. Roy looked at Buster's hooves.
"A horse vet has to know stuff that other veterinarians don't," he added.
"For example, the horse's hoof is like a big toenail.
The hoof is hard on the outside, but the inside is easily hurt."
"Did you go to a different school to learn about horses?"
"No. I worked a lot with horses in veterinary school."
Dr. Roy looked in Buster's mouth.
"Some vets even decide to study a specialty, like horse dentistry or surgery."
"Wow," Jessica said.
Buster coughed and thick liquid ran from his nose.
Dr. Roy listened to Buster's throat with the stethoscope.
"I think Buster has a cold. I'll have to check his temperature to be sure."
"Horses get colds?"
"Of course. Horses get colds the same way you do—viruses spread from horse to horse.
Humans can prevent colds by washing their hands.
But horses can't do that!
So we prevent horse colds by keeping stalls and water clean."
"I hate when my nose gets stuffy," Jessica said.
"I have to breathe through my mouth!"
"Horses can only breathe through their noses," said Dr. Roy.
"Poor Buster." Jessica stroked the horse's nose.
"Does he need medicine?"
"Buster just needs rest and lots of water," Dr. Roy said, smiling.
Just then Mr. Petersen appeared.
"Ginger's all ready for you, Jessica!"
"Okay . . ." Jessica looked back at Dr. Roy and Buster.
"When can I ride Buster again?" she asked.
"You can probably ride him again in three to four weeks," Dr. Roy said.
"He needs at least one week of rest for every day that he had a fever."
"That's a long time," Jessica said, disappointed.
"Feel better, Buster."
"Don't be too sad," Dr. Roy called after her.
"You'll like Ginger. She's my favorite!"
One afternoon Mrs. Hamilton was making dinner.
Suddenly an uninvited guest scurried into her kitchen.
"Eek! There's a mouse!
There's a mouse!" screamed Mrs. Hamilton.
"Are you all right, dear?" asked Mr. Hamilton.
"No, I am not all right.
There is a mouse in my house!" Mrs. Hamilton said angrily.
"What should we do?" asked Jason.
"I've got it!" Mr. Hamilton said suddenly. "We'll get a cat!"
The next day Mr. Hamilton went to buy a cat.
"Did you get the cat?"
asked Jason when Mr. Hamilton got home.
A little head appeared from Mr. Hamilton's arms.
"Meow," it said in a tiny voice.
"Hello, cat!" said Jason.
"You need a name since you will be part of the family."
Jason and Mr. Hamilton tried to think of a name for a long time.
Finally Mr. Hamilton said, "I know.
We will call you Snatch since you will snatch up the mice in our house."
Later that day Jason began to train the cat to catch mice.
He showed Snatch a little toy mouse.
"This is a mouse," he said.
"When you see a mouse, pounce on it."
Snatch was a very active cat.
She loved to chase butterflies and birds.
"Look how fast she is!" Mr. Hamilton said proudly.
Mrs. Hamilton held a treat in her hand.
Then Snatch jumped up to eat it.
"Look how high she can jump!" Mrs. Hamilton said proudly.
Snatch learned quickly.
Jason liked to test her when she didn't know he was there.
"Snatch! It's a mouse!"
Jason threw the toy mouse for Snatch to catch.
"Look how smart she is!" cried Jason proudly.
"She is so fast," said Mr. Hamilton.
"She is so strong," said Mrs. Hamilton.
"She is so smart," said Jason.
Mrs. Hamilton went to the kitchen to get some ice cream.
"Yeek! It's a mouse! It's a mouse!" she screamed.
Everyone ran into the kitchen.
"Go, Snatch! Get the mouse!" they cried.
Snatch chased the mouse into a corner.
The mouse was trapped!
"Good work, Snatch!" shouted the family.
Snatch got closer to the mouse.
Suddenly the little mouse bit Snatch on the nose.
Snatch meowed and ran out of the room.
The Hamiltons were disappointed.
The Hamiltons held a family meeting.
"What do we do now?" asked Mrs. Hamilton.
Everyone wanted to get rid of the mouse, but now Snatch was afraid of mice.
So the next day, Mr. Hamilton put out a mousetrap.
"I thought all cats caught mice," said Jason.
"I guess not," said Mr. Hamilton.
Snatch was not good at catching real mice, but everyone loved her anyway.
Annie was excited, along with everyone else in her class.
The children were getting ready to start rehearsing for their annual play.
This year the play was The Three Billy Goats Gruff
. Their teacher, Ms. Fisher, had been reading the story to them for weeks now, and they all knew it by
heart. Everyone wanted to be in the
play. Everyone, that is, except
Henry. "I just want to stand in the corner and be a tree," Henry told
Annie. "Come on, Henry! Being in a play will be fun!" Annie
said. Ms. Fisher tried to get the children to quiet
down. "I need everyone to
listen! We’re going to have our first rehearsal
now. Who knows what a rehearsal
is?" Annie raised her
hand. "It’s when we practice for the
play." "Yes, Annie. This year, everyone is going to have a speaking part, so we have to practice saying our lines," said Ms.
Fisher. "Nobody will stand around as a
tree. There are four
parts: the first goat, the second goat, the third goat, and the
troll. Everyone will share a
part. I’ve already chosen who will play
what." Someone called out, "I know what Henry is going to be—the
troll!" All the children laughed except
Annie. "No, I’m not!" yelled Henry, as he ran under a
table. "I don’t want to be in a stupid
play!" Ms. Fisher said patiently, "Henry, if you stay under that table, you’ll miss our first
rehearsal. Then you can’t be in the
play. Don’t you want to join
us?" Henry shook his
head. "Okay, then you will sit in the corner and watch
us. You know where to
go," said Ms. Fisher, pointing to a chair in the corner of the
room. Henry sat in the chair and sadly watched the rest of the
class. Annie was chosen to be one of the first
goats. She wanted to make Henry feel
better. She tried smiling at
him. But he didn’t look at her.
Later, during lunch, Annie tried talking to Henry.
But he ignored her for the rest of the day.
He didn’t care if he had to sit in the corner during every rehearsal.
He would not be in the play.
The next day, the class rehearsed again.
The goats were practicing walking over the bridge while saying, "Trip, trap, trip, trap."
But Ms. Fisher wasn’t pleased.
She said, "Something is missing.
We need to make the goats’ footsteps louder.
Each goat should sound heavier than the one before it.
We’ll have to think of something."
Meanwhile, Annie was trying to think of how to make Henry interested in the play.
The kids had music class next.
They were all allowed to choose their instruments.
Annie chose the tambourine.
Henry chose the drum.
They paraded around the room with their instruments.
First they played softly.
Then they played loud, louder, and loudest of all.
When the class was over, the music teacher praised everyone, especially Henry.
"Wonderful, Henry! You did a great job playing the drum louder and louder each time."
Suddenly, Annie had an idea!
She hurried to Ms. Fisher to tell her.
The teacher liked the idea.
Then Ms. Fisher walked over to Henry and said,
"I heard you played the drum very well today, Henry—is that right?"
Henry smiled with pride.
"Would you like to play the drum during the play?
We need someone to make the sound of goats walking over the bridge."
Henry nodded his head excitedly.
"It’s not a speaking part," Ms. Fisher said, "but we would be happy if you joined us."
"We’re going to be in the play together!"
Annie shouted as she hugged Henry.
The play was a big success.
At the final curtain call, all the children lined up and bowed.
Henry and Annie looked at each other and smiled.
Annie gave Henry the thumbs-up.
"I knew you could do it!" she whispered.
Recess was Henry’s favorite part of the school day.
He liked to chase the other kids around the playground.
"Aaaaahhhhhh!" he screamed, making his scariest monster face.
When the kids saw Henry coming, they would shout,
"Here comes the monster!"
Then they would run away screaming and giggling.
Henry could be quite a few different monsters: a wolf, a gorilla, or a ghost.
He tried hard to make each one scary.
What Henry really wanted, though, was to play nicely like everyone else.
He wanted to make sand castles or play catch with the other kids.
But Henry was shy and talked in a quiet voice.
He was always afraid the other kids would laugh at him.
The only way he could play was by being a monster.
"Oh, Henry, can’t you play some other way?" Henry’s teacher asked him.
She tried showing him how to play in the sandbox, but Henry wasn’t good at making sand castles.
He always ended up throwing sand in other kids’ faces by accident.
One day, a new girl arrived at school.
Henry saw her sitting alone in a corner, looking sad.
He was curious.
"Maybe I can make her run away from me.
It might be fun," he thought.
He decided to be the ghost.
Slowly, he walked toward her, making scary faces and sounds.
But she didn’t even look at him.
He got closer and beat his chest, grunting like a gorilla.
She still did not move.
Then he showed his teeth and screamed as loud as he could.
The girl finally looked up at him.
She giggled and then laughed out loud.
Henry was confused.
The next thing she did confused him even more.
She opened her mouth wide and roared like a lion.
This had never happened before!
Kids were always scared of him!
What was he supposed to do?
The girl kept making funny faces and laughing.
Then Henry laughed too.
This was fun!
"I like playing monster!" said the girl.
"Do you want to see my wolf monster?" Henry asked proudly.
"Sure!"
Henry threw his head back and howled like a wolf. "Aooooo!"
"Wow! Let me try." The girl howled too.
"Aooooo! I’m Annie. What’s your name?"
"Henry."
"I’m glad you’re playing with me.
Everyone else already has a friend."
Then Henry shyly asked, "Do you want to be my friend?"
Annie smiled and gave Henry a hug.
"Yes! I’d love to be your friend!"
Henry blushed.
"Tag, you’re it!" Annie yelled as she ran away.
Henry and Annie chased each other happily around the playground.
They took turns being the scariest monster.
Then Annie taught Henry how to make sand castles in the sandbox.
Henry’s teacher was very happy.
Henry was happy too.
He did not have to be a monster all the time anymore.
Now, he and Annie were best friends.
Once there was a bear who lived in a meadow.
He was very big.
And he was always very hungry.
His name was Bo Bo.
One day, Bo Bo smelled honey.
He followed his nose to a tree.
Then he looked up.
There he saw a huge beehive hanging on a branch!
"My lucky day!" he said.
Carefully, Bo Bo climbed the tree.
And, carefully, he climbed out onto the branch.
But Bo Bo was too heavy.
The branch broke.
Down he fell, with the beehive, to the ground. THUMP!
The bees came out, and started to chase Bo Bo.
Bo Bo ran away.
He ran faster and faster.
"HELP ME!" he screamed. "Somebody help me!"
Freddy the frog heard Bo Bo screaming.
Then he saw the bees.
"Quick! Jump in the pond!" Freddy yelled.
Bo Bo jumped right in, and the bees flew away.
"Thank you!" said Bo Bo when he came up for air.
"You saved my life!"
"You're welcome," said Freddy kindly.
"This pond is my home.
You were lucky to be running this way.
Can I ask you a question?"
"Sure," said Bo Bo.
"Why were those bees chasing you?"
Bo Bo scratched his fuzzy head.
"I don't know. Maybe they were angry."
Freddy was smarter than most frogs.
And he was definitely smarter than Bo Bo.
"I bet you wanted their honey, right?" he asked.
"Oh yeah," Bo Bo remembered sadly.
Freddy thought for a moment.
He felt sorry for the bear.
Then he said, "Are you hungry?
I know where you can catch some tasty fish, and I can catch some tasty flies."
He licked his lips.
"Sure!" said Bo Bo happily.
He followed Freddy to a stream.
"There are lots of fish here," said Freddy.
"Just wait and you'll see."
Bo Bo waited. Soon he saw lots of fish.
Better than honey!
He jumped into the water to grab a fish.
But then he heard Freddy screaming.
Bo Bo dropped the fish.
He saw a snake hissing at Freddy.
"GRRRRRR!" Bo Bo growled at the snake.
The snake slipped away.
"Th-th-thank you," Freddy said, shaking all over.
"You saved my life."
"That's what friends are for.
They help each other," said Bo Bo.
"Does that mean we're friends now?"
"Yes, I think it does." Freddy smiled.
"Let's catch some dinner. I'm hungry."
They had a great time catching as many fish and flies as they wanted.
Freddy showed Bo Bo where all the fish were hiding.
And Bo Bo scared away the snakes.
The two friends sat on the bank of the stream, watching the sun set over the hill.
"I'm glad I met you," said Bo Bo.
"I'm glad I met you," said Freddy.
Then after a while he said, "This is only the beginning."
"The beginning of what?" asked Bo Bo.
"Of our friendship," said Freddy.
And they watched the sun set, feeling full and happy.

episodes.title: Marvin in the Deep Blue Sea

subtitle.text: Marvin was a goldfish who lived in a pond in Lily's backyard.
Every day, Lily would feed all the goldfish.
She loved to watch them swim about and gave each one a name.
Marvin was her favorite because he had an especially long and beautiful tail.
Marvin loved his home.
He loved to swim in the clear, green water and play among the lily pads and tall reeds.
Best of all, there was a waterfall.
The pond was just perfect.
Marvin couldn't imagine living anywhere else.
One day, Marvin heard a frog bragging about what he did outside the pond.
"There's way more to do out there," said the frog.
"More bugs to catch, and there are rabbits and squirrels─all kinds of new things to see." Suddenly,
the pond didn't seem so great anymore. But
Marvin was a fish. He
couldn't go anywhere without water. "Wait,"
he thought, "where is there more water than in this pond? The
sea! It's bigger than big!" He
thought of the fantastic sea creatures he'd meet, and the secret caves he'd discover. He
had to get there. Marvin
soon became grumpy. His
friends noticed. "Why
are you sad?" they asked. "I
don't like it here anymore. I
want to be out in the deep blue sea!" "Yeah,
in your dreams!" they laughed. But
Marvin wouldn't give up his dream. One
night, there was a rainstorm. The
water in the pond started to rise. "This
could be my only chance to get out of here!" thought Marvin. When
the water seemed high enough, he swam right over the rocks around the pond. He
was free! The
rainwater carried him to a stream, where he swam and swam. Suddenly,
a huge turtle dived in beside him. It
made such a big splash that Marvin sailed up in the air.
He landed in a puddle surrounded by tall weeds.
He was stuck!
Marvin was scared and all alone.
What was he going to do?
The next morning, Lily ran to the pond and found Marvin missing.
Her heart was broken.
Her parents tried to make her feel better.
"We'll get a new fish," they said, "one like Marvin."
Lily shook her head.
"No one could be like Marvin.
He was the best fish in the world."
Meanwhile, a boy was walking by the stream and saw Marvin trying to get out of the puddle.
He carefully scooped him up in a cup.
For what seemed like a very long time, Marvin was cramped in a small, dark container.
Then he was dumped into a crowded glass tank with strange fish.
Weird people would stare at him and tap on the glass.
"Oh, how I wish I were back in the pond again with my friends," sighed Marvin.
"This is terrible."
Days went by, and Marvin began to lose hope of ever going home again.
He began to sink lower and lower in the tank.
Pretty soon he just stayed on the bottom.
Then, to his amazement, he saw Lily!
Her parents had taken her to the pet store where Marvin had ended up.
She was looking at the fish in each of the tanks.
Marvin swam right up to the glass and wiggled his long tail back and forth as fast as he could, trying to get her attention.
"Mom and Dad, look!
I found Marvin!" Lily cried.
She brought him home right away.
Marvin was very happy to be back in the pond.
"Did you get to the sea?" his friends asked.
"It wasn't exactly what I thought it would be," he said with a sly grin.
"Home is much better."
He stood as silent and white as the snow.
His blue eyes were triangle-shaped.
They were old tiles from a wall or floor.
One eye hung close to his carrot nose.
A large old comb had become his mouth.
The uneven teeth made it appear as though he were frowning.
Inside, however, the snowman was smiling.
He was alive.
"My, how cold it is today," the snowman exclaimed happily.
"Woof! How can you be happy that it's cold?" barked Dog.
Even Dog's fur could not keep him warm.
"What do you mean?" Snowman was confused.
"Everyone loves the cold winter.
Just look at those children!"
Three boys were having a snowball fight.
Other children rode down a hill on sleds.
They were all shouting with joy.
"See? The cold makes everyone feel alive!" said Snowman.
"Woof! Not everyone likes the cold."
Dog lifted his head toward the shining sun.
The sun's rays beamed down on the icy snow.
Drops of water formed where the warm rays touched the snow.
"What is that?"
Snowman asked as he looked up at the sky.
Snowman did not feel comfortable.
"It is called the sun," Dog answered.
"See how it glows?
It can melt away all this snow."
"Melt? That sounds horrible," gasped Snowman.
"I won't let it melt me."
Dog barked and barked.
It sounded as though he were laughing.
"We'll see about that!" Dog said nastily.
Turning around three times, Dog went inside his doghouse.
Snowman continued to watch the playful children.
"I wish I could slide the way they do," he thought to himself.
All day, Snowman stood still and silent.
He did not dare look up at the sky.
He knew Sun was there staring at him.
"I won't let Sun get me," Snowman said firmly.
"Children love the snow."
Shortly after, something wonderful happened.
Sun slowly disappeared.
"I won! I won!" Snowman shouted.
If he had had legs, Snowman would have jumped for joy.
"Woof! What are you shouting for?"
Dog came out of his house, yawning and stretching.
"Look! Sun has gone away.
And it didn't melt me!" Snowman cried.
If he had had arms, Snowman would have waved to the sky.
Again Dog laughed and laughed.
"Sun will be back tomorrow.
But now Moon, his friend, is here."
Dog looked up at the dark sky and howled.
Snowman carefully looked up.
Indeed, a white round ball had replaced Sun.
"Can Moon melt snow too?" asked Snowman.
"Of course not," barked Dog. "But Moon keeps shining.
So tomorrow Sun will know where you are."
Snowman felt afraid.
He looked around.
The children were all gone too.
"I'm all alone," he said sadly.
"Well, too bad," barked Dog.
"I would stay but it's time for my dinner."
Dog trotted toward the house.
He barked and scratched at the door.
A young boy opened it and Dog disappeared inside.
All night, Snowman stood still and silent.
Early the next morning, just as Dog had said, Sun was back.
"So you have returned," Snowman said to Sun.
"Well, you won't melt me today, either!" Snowman shouted.
Snowman watched as children came out to play again.
Some stopped to look at him.
"His eye is falling," a little girl said.
She pulled the hanging tile off.
Then she shoved it next to the other one.
"Thank you. Now I can see much better," Snowman thought.
Snowman was very happy.
"Little children must like me," he said to himself.
"They come up to me and smile."
"Excuse me," a small voice called from below.
Snowman looked down.
It was a little rabbit.
"Yes?" Snowman said.
"It's very cold," began Rabbit.
"It is indeed," Snowman said happily.
"I can't find any food to eat.
I just wish this horrible winter would end," cried Rabbit.
Suddenly, he saw Snowman's nose.
"My, what a fine nose you have," said Rabbit.
He licked his lips.
Snowman looked down at his carrot nose.
Then he looked at Rabbit.
Rabbit did look cold and thin.
"Do you want my nose?" Snowman asked.
"Oh, would you mind?" Rabbit asked eagerly.
"Not at all," Snowman said kindly.
Rabbit plucked the carrot off.
"Thank you so much!" Rabbit waved and hopped away.
So once again, Snowman was alone.
Sun stayed out all day.
But he could not melt Snowman.
Then Moon came out again.
"I'm still here!" laughed Snowman.
"Your friend Sun couldn't melt me!"
Moon remained silent but he kept his light on Snowman.
Day and night, Sun and Moon took turns shining down on Snowman.
Day and night, Snowman tried to keep standing straight.
Then one day, something happened.
"I don't feel so good," Snowman said to Dog.
Dog had not gone into the house that night.
He stayed in his house outside.
"That's because the weather is changing," barked Dog.
"Changing? But why? Everyone loves winter," Snowman cried.
"Maybe," said Dog, "but everyone loves spring too."
"Spring? What is that?" Snowman asked.
"Spring is the time for flowers and trees to blossom.
Grass grows back," explained Dog.
"But what about the snow?
What about me?" Snowman asked quietly.
Dog laughed and laughed.
"I told you! Sun will melt you away."
Snowman looked down.
There was a growing puddle around his body.
"But don't worry," barked Dog.
"You'll be back next winter."
"I will?" asked Snowman.
"Yes, you come back every winter," said Dog.
Snowman thought about Dog's words.
"Will I see you next winter?" he asked.
Dog turned around three times.
"Of course!" he barked and went inside his house.
"Good-bye, friend," Snowman called out.
Then he slowly disappeared.
One day, a master took his two friendly dogs out for a walk.
The dogs were having an energetic time running about and soon they became completely lost.
After several hours, the dogs became hungry, so they agreed to split up.
One dog went to the first town and the other to the second town in search of food.
The dogs were certain that people would give them something to eat.
When the first dog arrived in town, he was very excited.
There were many fancy houses and stores.
He ran up to the first store and barked happily for some food.
But the man in the store yelled at him.
He thought the man was very strange, so he went up to a nice-looking house.
However, the woman there screamed and shouted at him.
Her husband came out and hit the dog with a broom.
That really hurt.
The dog was in pain and getting a little angry.
Slowly, he walked to another house.
There, to his delight, was a big juicy steak sitting beside a barbecue.
The dog ran and jumped for the steak.
However, before he could get it, a man grabbed him and threw him back onto the street.
The man shouted at him and chased him down the street.
Even the neighborhood children began to throw rocks at him.
This made the dog very angry.
Within a few days, the dog became mean and wild.
He barked and growled at the children.
He chased the women in the streets and stole food from the houses and stores.
He became a terrible menace in the little town.
People lived in fear of the dog.
Mothers had to walk their children to school because they were worried that the terrible dog would bite them.
In a short time, the dog had made the wonderful little town a terrible place to live.
In the meantime, the other dog went to the second town.
This was also a nice town with good houses and stores.
At the first store, the owner felt very sorry for the dog and gave him a small piece of meat.
The dog barked with joy.
As he was passing a home, a woman came out to play with him.
She petted the dog and gave him a little bit of food.
The dog was delighted at this.
He rolled over and did many tricks that humans like to watch.
Children came up to him and he played with them.
Soon the dog became very well-known and loved in town.
People would give him food, and some even let him sleep in their garages at night.
The dog also protected the children when they walked to school.
He watched over the people of the town and they watched over him.
For many years in that small town, there was more love because of that dog.
Which town are you from?
Are you from a town that treats strangers and newcomers badly or do you welcome newcomers and treat them with respect?
Long ago, a wealthy landowner lived in Louisiana.
His name was Charles Durance.
He had two daughters who were getting married.
Their weddings were planned for the same day at their father's farm.
Mr. Durance loved his daughters very much.
So, he decided to prepare a big surprise for them.
"My daughters' weddings are coming up.
Is there a way to make it a special day for them?" he wondered.
After days of thinking, he came up with a wonderful idea.
He went to talk to his servants.
"I need lots of spiders.
Where can I get some?" he asked.
"You can probably get them from China," one of his servants replied.
"How many spiders do you need?"
"I need millions of them," said Mr. Durance.
The servants were surprised.
"Spiders are expensive.
They will have to come on a ship from China," one servant explained.
Charles ordered the spiders anyway.
Several months later, a shipload of spiders arrived from China.
"What shall we do with all the spiders?" the servants asked Mr. Durance.
"Let them loose in the trees along the road to the house," he instructed.
"Why are we letting all of these spiders loose?" they wondered.
"It's almost time for his daughters' weddings."
Mr. Durance's servants were puzzled.
Over the next few days, the spiders spun webs throughout the trees.
Mr. Durance called his servants.
"I want you to go into town.

The servants were puzzled and curious.

Charles Durance was very satisfied.

Mr. Durance's instructions surprised the servants again.
But they did as he said and sprinkled the powder on the webs.
When they were finished, they saw what Charles Durance had planned.
The spider webs along the road sparkled in the sunlight.

My father was a traveling salesman for a long time.
In those days, there were quite a few traveling salesmen.
They sold tools, encyclopedias, records, and even chocolate!
My father sold small tools and toolboxes.
He traveled to small towns and villages in the Midwest.
Sometimes, he would have to drive for hundreds of miles!
He'd show people the latest products and how they worked.
He told me that, on the whole, he was pretty successful.
He loved meeting new people each day, and he enjoyed his work very much.
One time, my father entered a very small town as it was getting dark.
He noticed that the town had only one street, with a few small stores.
He went into the only store with a light on to ask for directions to a hotel.
"Good evening, sir," my father began.
"Evenin' to you!" replied the storekeeper.
"I'm looking for a hotel."
"Well, you just found it."
"Is this a hotel?
I didn't see any signs," asked my dad.
"Yep. Mine is the only one.
Do you need a room?"
"Sure."
"Come this way," said the man.
The hotel manager led the way to a small, dark room in the corner.
"Do you have anything bigger?" asked my dad.
"Nope. In fact, this is the only room we have."
"I'll take it then," my dad replied.
Later that evening, my dad realized that he hadn't had a meal all day.
So he made his way back to the hotel manager.
"Do you serve dinner?" he asked.
"Yep, in the other room."
"What time?"
"Come when you like," said the hotel manager.
After my dad unpacked, he made his way to the "other room," which was supposed to be the dining room.
To my father's surprise, the hotel manager was also the waiter!
He asked, "Will you have sausage on toast?"
"No, I never eat sausage," replied my dad.
"In that case," said the waiter, "dinner is over."
Disappointed with the choice of food in the dining room, my father skipped his meal.
He returned to his room.
The next morning, my father searched for the hotel manager to pay for his stay.
He looked throughout the hotel.
He found the manager asleep in his bathrobe on a living room chair.
At that moment, my father realized that he wasn't in a hotel after all!
He had spent the entire night in this stranger's home.

Luke and I have been best friends since we were in the first grade.
We did everything together.
We played basketball and rode our bikes.
We went swimming together in the summer.
Sometimes I would even sleep over at Luke's house.
But last year, something really terrible happened to Luke.
One day, he was riding his bicycle to the park.
He was riding really fast because he was late for his baseball game.
So, when Luke came to the big road, he couldn't stop.
Luke went right out into the middle of the road.
There was a car coming, and the driver couldn't stop either.
The car ran right into my friend Luke.
The ambulance had to come and take Luke to the hospital.
Luke was really sick and he had to stay in the hospital for three months.
Finally, after waiting for one month, I was allowed to visit him in the hospital.
I was so excited I asked my mom if I could buy Luke a present.
I thought he would like a new soccer ball.
Then my mom told me the bad news.
"Luke cannot use a soccer ball now.
Because of his accident, Luke cannot walk," she said.
"What do you mean?" I cried.
"If Luke can't walk, then how can he play with me?
Who will I play basketball with?" I said to my mother.
Then I began to cry.
"You can still play with Luke," my mother said.
"I can't play with him," I replied.
"How can he play if he can't walk?"
For many days, I didn't go to the hospital to see Luke.
I became very lonely and sad.
I tried to play basketball, but it wasn't any fun.
I went swimming, but it was boring.
Then I thought of Luke.
I realized that Luke must be even sadder and more bored than I.
So finally, one Saturday morning, I went to visit Luke in the hospital.
I arrived at the hospital, and slowly I walked toward his door.
But I was really scared.
I had never talked to a person who had been hurt in an accident.
What would I say to him?
Maybe he would not want to be friends with me.
Maybe he'd be mean and angry.
When I knocked, I heard a familiar voice say, "Who's there?"
"It's Richard," I responded.
I opened his door, and there he was, sitting in a wheelchair.
I didn't know what to say to him, and I wanted to run away.
"Watch this!" he shouted.
"I can make my wheelchair go on two wheels.
Do you want to see?"
"Sure," I replied quietly.
Soon Luke and I were racing up and down the halls at the hospital.
Then the nurse got mad and told us to stop, so we played with Luke's new video game.
We had lots of fun that day.
I learned that Luke was the same friend I had always had.
I felt a little ashamed that I didn't visit him earlier, but I was glad I went to the hospital that day.
When Luke came out of the hospital, he wanted to do all the old things we used to do.
He wanted to play basketball, and he wanted to play baseball.
At first he couldn't do any of these things, so sometimes Luke would get angry, and sometimes he would be sad.
But slowly, Luke learned how to play without his legs.
He learned to play basketball by using a special sports wheelchair.
He learned how to swim without using his legs.
Today, with help from his family and friends, Luke can usually do whatever he wants.
Of course, Luke has changed a bit since his accident, but he is still a great person.
And he is definitely still my friend.

She wanted to search the area for clues.

Annie opened the cupboard.
One of the cups was missing.
Annie opened the lid to the garbage can.
She found the wrapper from her cake.
